title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks - Guidance
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's standards and practical guidance for SRE-owned reliability work: SLO definitions and error budget policies, capacity planning and forecasting, reliability initiatives prioritization, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbooks for common production problems. The goal is to ensure predictable availability and latency for inference services while keeping operational overhead and unit cost on target.

Scope

- Applies to all Redwood-hosted inference services (text-generation, chat, embeddings, reranking) and the internal control plane used for routing/observability.
- Includes both customer-facing and internal platform endpoints.
- Excludes third-party managed services where SLAs are contractually defined; those are tracked separately under procurement.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

SLO design principles:
- Measure user-facing correctness: prefer client-observed SLI where possible (API success rate, end-to-end latency).
- Separate availability and latency SLOs for distinct user experiences (sync generation, streaming, embeddings).
- Use 30d rolling windows for operational alerts and 90d windows for quarterly reliability reviews.
- Keep SLOs actionable: tie error budget burn to concrete mitigations (rollback, scaling, capacity reserve).

Primary SLOs (example canonical definitions):

- Text-generation (sync endpoints):
  - SLI: percent of requests that complete with HTTP 200 and model response delivered within 600ms (p95)
  - Target: 99.95% over 30d

- Chat / streaming responses:
  - SLI: percent of session-level streams that sustain per-chunk latency below 100ms (p95) and do not terminate unexpectedly
  - Target: 99.9% over 30d

- Embeddings (batch and single-call):
  - SLI: percent of embedding requests that complete within 250ms (single) / 3s (batch 64) and return valid vectors
  - Target: 99.9% over 30d

- Control-plane (routing/metadata):
  - SLI: API availability for route management and key operations (create/update routes) within 300ms (p95)
  - Target: 99.99% over 30d

Error budget accounting and burn policies:
- Error budget = (1 - SLO_target) * measurement_window. Example: for 99.95% SLO over 30d, daily budget = 0.05% * 30d equivalent.
- Continuous burn tracking with burn-rate alerts (5x, 10x, and 20x on 6h windows) triggers progressively escalatory actions.
- Actions by burn-rate tier:
  - 5x sustained for 6h: Pager -> SRE on-call investigate; temporary mitigation checklist (throttle low-priority routes, increase capacity pools).
  - 10x sustained for 6h: Incident declared, engineering pager rota; consider rollback/traffic diversion to fallback models/regions.
  - 20x sustained or catastrophic outage: Executive incident declared; follow major-incident runbook and customer comms templates.

2) Capacity Planning and Forecasting

Capacity metrics to track (per service/model/region):
- QPS (requests/sec) and tokens/sec
- Concurrent requests and session counts (streaming sessions)
- GPU utilization per instance (p50/p95), memory pressure, and PCIe bandwidth
- Average request size (tokens) and p95/p99 length distribution
- Cold start / model load time and KV cache hit rates
- Autoscaler actions per minute and scale latency

Forecasting process (quarterly, with monthly refresh):
1. Baseline demand: take 90d rolling average QPS and annotate recent growth signals (product releases, marketing, known customer onboardings).
2. Scenario modelling: produce three scenarios for the upcoming quarter: base (+10% w/seasonality), high (+40%), and surge (+100%).
3. Capacity gap analysis: convert QPS/tokens into GPU-hours using conservative inference efficiency numbers per model (documented in model catalog). Include buffer (safety margin) aligned to business SLA tier:
  - Hosted: 25% buffer
  - Dedicated: 15% buffer (customer reserved)
  - Private: customer-managed (recommendations only)
4. Procurement/ops action: schedule reserved capacity purchases or region bursts if projected deficits exceed buffer for the high scenario.
5. Validate with load tests: run canary traffic and 2x spike tests during the release window.

Capacity runbook (short):
- On sustained >70% p95 GPU utilization for 4h:
  1. Notify SRE channel and on-call.
  2. Check autoscaler events and recent deployment rollouts.
  3. Increase instance pool by +20% for affected model variants (manual scale if autoscaler unstable).
  4. If scaling limited, enable traffic shaping: route non-critical traffic to lower-cost model variants or enable aggressive batching for low-latency workloads.
  5. Post-incident: record capacity burn in quarterly forecast and update procurement plan.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

Common high-impact initiatives (examples):
- KV cache persistence improvements to increase cache hit rate by 10-30% and reduce token re-compute.
- Adaptive batching: dynamic batch size selection by observed request length and latency SLO to reduce GPU-hours.
- Autoscaler improvements: reduce scale latency from minutes to seconds for streaming workloads.
- Fallback model family: maintain low-cost, lower-capacity model variants and test automatic fallback policies.
- Better model startup (checkpoint warmers) to reduce cold-starts for rare variants.

Prioritization criteria:
- SLO impact: expected reduction in error budget burn
- Cost impact: expected reduction in $/token or $/QPS
- Operational risk reduction: fewer manual interventions or simpler on-call runbooks
- Implementation effort (weeks) and cross-team dependencies

4) Incident Review Standards and Postmortem Structure

Incident classification and severity (S0- S3):
- S0 (Major outage): Extended widespread customer-impacting degradation or severely compromised data integrity.
- S1 (Partial outage): Large subset of customers affected or severe degradation for specific regions/models.
- S2 (Minor degradation): Limited impact, degraded performance for small customer segments.
- S3 (No end-user impact): Internal tooling or metrics issues only.

Postmortem template (required fields):
1. Summary: one-paragraph user-impact summary.
2. Timeline: concise event timeline with clocked timestamps.
3. Impact: metrics (requests failed, p95 latency delta, error-budget burn, affected customers/regions).
4. Root cause analysis: technical cause(s) with evidence (logs, traces, profiling).
5. Detection: how the incident was detected (alert, customer report, internal dashboard).
6. Mitigation steps taken and rationale.
7. Corrective actions: short-term (<=7d) and long-term (>7d) action items with owners and due dates.
8. Lessons learned and follow-ups: documentation or runbook updates.
9. Post-incident SLO recalculation and error budget reconciliation.

Postmortem rules:
- All S1+ incidents must have a postmortem within 5 business days.
- Blameless language required; focus on systemic fixes.
- Action items must have an owner and due date; SRE manager verifies completion at 30d.

5) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

Minimum dashboard and alerting expectations per service:
- Key dashboards: SLO overview (error budget, burn rate), latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), capacity view (GPU utilization, queue length), traffic breakdown by model/route/region, recent deploys and autoscaler events.
- Pager alerts: only for actionable, noisy-filtered signals tied to SLOs or systemic failures. Examples:
  - Error rate > SLO threshold for 10 min (pager)
  - Burn rate > 5x on 6h window (pager)
  - p95 latency > target for 10 min and sustained traffic (pager)
  - GPU OOM / instance termination (pager)
- Composite alerts: combine symptom + upstream cause signals to reduce false positives (e.g., high latency + sustained CPU steal on orchestration host).
- Observability features required: request-level tracing, token-level cost attribution, and per-model rollout tracing.

Tooling owned by SRE platform team:
- SLO and error budget dashboards (single pane for SRE leads and product owners)
- Capacity planner app: accepts traffic inputs, simulates capacity needs by model and SKU
- On-call runbook portal: searchable runbooks, postmortem links, and runbook ownership metadata

6) Canonical Runbooks (examples)

Runbook: High latency on text-generation sync endpoint
- Symptoms: p95 latency > 600ms for >10m, error budget burn-rate > 3x, customer reports of slow responses.
- Triage steps:
  1. Confirm SLO breach on SLO dashboard and identify affected region/model variants.
  2. Check recent deploys (last 60m) and autoscaler activity. If deployment occurred, roll back to previous stable revision.
  3. Inspect GPU utilization and queue length. If GPU p95 > 80% and queue > expected, scale pool by +25%.
  4. Check KV cache hit-rate; if hit-rate drop corresponds to latency spike, invalidate / warm cache for hot prefixes.
  5. If scaling not possible, route new traffic to fallback model variant (documented in routing table) and throttle large batch jobs.
- Mitigation and communication:
  - Post short incident update to status page and customer-facing channel within 30m for S1/S0 incidents.
  - If rollback or routing change applied, monitor p95 and error budget for 30m before declaring resolved.
  - Run a targeted load test to validate fix under controlled conditions.

Runbook: High GPU error / OOM on inference node
- Symptoms: GPU driver errors, container OOM, node termination, increased 5xx rate.
- Steps:
  1. Isolate instance: drain new traffic and run health-checks.
  2. Capture logs (dmesg, nv_crash logs), container runtime errors, and kernel OOM reports.
  3. If reproducible on single model variant, remove model variant from rotation and route to fallback.
  4. If hardware degradation suspected, mark instance for replacement and update capacity forecast.

Ownership and Governance

- SLO steward: assigned per-service (Product + SRE co-owned). SRE maintains instrumentation and alerts; Product signs off on SLO targets.
- Capacity lead: SRE platform manager coordinates quarterly capacity reviews with Finance and Cloud ops.
- Incident commander roster: defined in on-call rota; major incidents require a post-incident review with engineering and product stakeholders.

Operational cadence
- Weekly: SRE sync — review top 3 burners, open action items, and urgent runbook updates.
- Monthly: SLO review and error budget reconciliation per service.
- Quarterly: Capacity planning cycle with forecast sign-off and procurement requests.
- Post-incident: 5-day postmortem and 30-day action verification.

Appendices

A. SLO definition checklist:
- User-visible metric defined
- Measurement window and aggregation defined
- Measurement system and owner identified
- Alert thresholds and escalation policy mapped to burn rates

B. Useful commands and links
- SLO dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/slo-dashboard (internal)
- Capacity planner: https://tools.redwood.ai/capacity-planner
- On-call runbooks index: https://wiki.redwood.ai/runbooks
- Example query:
  - Grafana: request_count{env="prod",service="generation"} / rate_window(30d)

C. Template: short postmortem (copy into incident ticket)
- Title: [S1] Short one-line summary
- Impact: bullets with metrics and customer count
- Timeline: HH:MM UTC entries
- Root cause: one-paragraph
- Action items: owner | description | due date

If you have questions about applying these standards to a specific service or model family, ping the SRE leads (sre-leads@redwood.ai) or create an RFC in the eng-sre space.
